title: Exploiting Cloze Questions for Few Shot Text Classification and Natural Language Inference

sections.title: Abstract
sections.text: Some NLP tasks can be solved in a fully unsupervised fashion by providing a pretrained language model with "task descriptions" in natural language . While this approach underperforms its supervised counterpart, we show in this work that the two ideas can be combined: We introduce Pattern-Exploiting Training (Pet), a semi-supervised training procedure that reformulates input examples as cloze-style phrases to help language models understand a given task. These phrases are then used to assign soft labels to a large set of unlabeled examples. Finally, standard supervised training is performed on the resulting training set. For several tasks and languages, Pet outperforms supervised training and strong semi-supervised approaches in low-resource settings by a large margin. .

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text: Learning from examples is the predominant approach for many NLP tasks: A model is trained on a set of labeled examples from which it then generalizes to unseen data. Due to the vast number of languages, domains and tasks and the cost of annotating data, it is common in real-world uses of NLP to have only a small number of labeled examples, making few-shot learning a highly important research area. Unfortunately, applying standard supervised learning to small training sets often performs poorly; many problems are difficult to grasp from just looking at a few examples. For instance, assume we are given the following pieces of text: : This was the best pizza I've ever had. : You can get better sushi for half the price. : Pizza was average. Not worth the price. Furthermore, imagine we are told that the labels of and are and , respectively, and we are asked to infer the correct label for . Based only on these examples, this is impossible because plausible justifications can be found for both and . However, if we know that the underlying task is to identify whether the text says anything about prices, we can easily assign to . (1) A number of patterns encoding some form of task description are created to convert training examples to cloze questions; for each pattern, a pretrained language model is finetuned. (2) The ensemble of trained models annotates unlabeled data. (3) A classifier is trained on the resulting soft-labeled dataset. With the rise of pretrained language models (PLMs) such as GPT , BERT and RoBERTa , the idea of providing task descriptions has become feasible for neural architectures: We can simply append such descriptions in natural language to an input and let the PLM predict continuations that solve the task . So far, this idea has mostly been considered in zero-shot scenarios where no training data is available at all. In this work, we show that providing task descriptions can successfully be combined with standard supervised learning in few-shot settings: We introduce Pattern-Exploiting Training (Pet), a semi-supervised training procedure that uses natural language patterns to reformulate input examples into cloze-style phrases. As illustrated in Figure , Pet works in three steps: First, for each pattern a separate PLM is finetuned on a small training set . The ensemble of all models is then used to annotate a large unlabeled dataset with soft labels. Finally, a standard classifier is trained on the soft-labeled dataset. We also devise iPet, an iterative variant of Pet in which this process is repeated with increasing training set sizes. On a diverse set of tasks in multiple languages, we show that given a small to medium number of labeled examples, Pet and iPet substantially outperform unsupervised approaches, supervised training and strong semi-supervised baselines.

sections.title: Related Work
sections.text: provide hints in the form of natural language patterns for zero-shot learning of challenging tasks such as reading comprehension and question answering (QA). This idea has been applied to unsupervised text classification , commonsense knowledge mining and argumentative relation classification . use task descriptions for zero-shot classification but require a semantic parser. For relation extraction, automatically identify patterns that express given relations. rephrase several tasks as QA problems. frame various problems as language modeling tasks, but their patterns only loosely resemble natural language and are unsuitable for few-shot learning. Another recent line of work uses cloze-style phrases to probe the knowledge that PLMs acquire during pretraining; this includes probing for factual and commonsense knowledge , linguistic capabilities , understanding of rare words , and ability to perform symbolic reasoning . consider the problem of finding the best pattern to express a given task. Other approaches for few-shot learning in NLP include exploiting examples from related tasks and using data augmentation ; the latter commonly relies on back-translation , requiring large amounts of parallel data. Approaches using textual class descriptors typically assume that abundant examples are available for a subset of classes . In contrast, our approach requires no additional labeled data and provides an intuitive interface to leverage task-specific human knowledge. The idea behind iPet -- training multiple generations of models on data labeled by previous generations -- bears resemblance to self-training and bootstrapping approaches for word sense disambiguation , relation extraction , parsing , machine translation , and sequence generation .

sections.title: Pattern-Exploiting Training
sections.text: Let be a masked language model with vocabulary and mask token , and let be a set of labels for our target classification task . We write an input for task as a sequence of phrases with ; for example, if is textual inference (two input sentences). We define a pattern to be a function that takes as input and outputs a phrase or sentence that contains exactly one mask token, i.e., its output can be viewed as a cloze question. Furthermore, we define a verbalizer as an injective function that maps each label to a word from 's vocabulary. We refer to as a pattern-verbalizer pair (PVP). Using a PVP enables us to solve task as follows: Given an input , we apply to obtain an input representation , which is then processed by to determine the label for which is the most likely substitute for the mask. For example, consider the task of identifying whether two sentences and contradict each other (label ) or agree with each other ( ). For this task, we may choose the pattern a b combined with a verbalizer that maps to "Yes" and to "No". Given an example input pair the task now changes from having to assign a label without inherent meaning to answering whether the most likely choice for the masked position in is "Yes" or "No".

sections.title: Auxiliary Language Modeling
sections.text: In our application scenario, only a few training examples are available and catastrophic forgetting can occur. As a PLM finetuned for some PVP is still a language model at its core, we address this by using language modeling as auxiliary task. With denoting cross-entropy loss and language modeling loss, we compute the final loss as L = (1 - ) L_CE + L_MLM This idea was recently applied by in a data-rich scenario. As is typically much larger than , in preliminary experiments, we found a small value of to consistently give good results, so we use it in all our experiments. To obtain sentences for language modeling, we use the unlabeled set . However, we do not train directly on each , but rather on , where we never ask the language model to predict anything for the masked slot.

sections.title: Combining PVPs
sections.text: A key challenge for our approach is that in the absence of a large development set, it is hard to identify which PVPs perform well. To address this, we use a strategy similar to knowledge distillation . First, we define a set of PVPs that intuitively make sense for a given task . We then use these PVPs as follows: We finetune a separate language model for each as described in Section . As is small, this finetuning is cheap even for a large number of PVPs. We use the ensemble of finetuned models to annotate examples from . We first combine the unnormalized class scores for each example as where and the are weighting terms for the PVPs. We experiment with two different realizations of this weighing term: either we simply set for all or we set to be the accuracy obtained using on the training set before training. We refer to these two variants as uniform and weighted. use a similar idea in a zero-shot setting. We transform the above scores into a probability distribution using softmax. Following , we use a temperature of to obtain a suitably soft distribution. All pairs are collected in a (soft-labeled) training set . We finetune a PLM with a standard sequence classification head on . The finetuned model then serves as our classifier for . sections.title: Iterative Pet (iPet)
sections.text: Distilling the knowledge of all individual models into a single classifier means they cannot learn from each other. As some patterns perform (possibly much) worse than others, the training set for our final model may therefore contain many mislabeled examples. To compensate for this shortcoming, we devise iPet, an iterative variant of Pet. The core idea of iPet is to train several generations of models on datasets of increasing size. To this end, we first enlarge the original dataset by labeling selected examples from using a random subset of trained Pet models (Figure a). We then train a new generation of Pet models on the enlarged dataset (b); this process is repeated several times (c). More formally, let be the initial set of Pet models finetuned on , where each is trained for some PVP . We train generations of models where and each is trained for on its own training set . In each iteration, we multiply the training set size by a fixed constant while maintaining the label ratio of the original dataset. That is, with denoting the number of examples with label in , each contains examples with label . This is achieved by generating each as follows: We obtain by randomly choosing models from the previous generation with being a hyperparameter. Using this subset, we create a labeled dataset For each , we obtain by randomly choosing examples with label from . To avoid training future generations on mislabeled data, we prefer examples for which the ensemble of models is confident in its prediction. The underlying intuition is that even without calibration, examples for which labels are predicted with high confidence are typically more likely to be classified correctly . Therefore, when drawing from , we set the probability of each proportional to . We define . As can easily be verified, this dataset contains examples for each . After training generations of Pet models, we use to create and train as in basic Pet. With minor adjustments, iPet can even be used in a zero-shot setting. To this end, we define to be the set of untrained models and for all so that is trained on 10 examples evenly distributed across all labels. As may not contain enough examples for some label , we create all by sampling from the 100 examples for which is the highest, even if . For each subsequent generation, we proceed exactly as in basic iPet.

sections.title: Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate Pet on four English datasets: Yelp Reviews, AG's News, Yahoo Questions and MNLI . Additionally, we use x-stance to investigate how well Pet works for other languages. For all experiments on English, we use RoBERTa large as language model; for x-stance, we use XLM-R . We investigate the performance of Pet and all baselines for different training set sizes; each model is trained three times using different seeds and average results are reported. As we consider a few-shot setting, we assume no access to a large development set on which hyperparameters could be optimized. Our choice of hyperparameters is thus based on choices made in previous work and practical considerations. We use a learning rate of , a batch size of and a maximum sequence length of . Unless otherwise specified, we always use the weighted variant of Pet with auxiliary language modeling. For iPet, we set and ; that is, we select of all models to label examples for the next generation and quintuple the number of training examples in each iteration. We train new generations until each model was trained on at least examples, i.e., we set . As we always repeat training three times, the ensemble (or ) for PVPs contains models. Further hyperparameters and detailed explanations for all our choices are given in Appendix B.

sections.title: Results
sections.text: English Datasets Table shows results for English text classification and language understanding tasks; we report mean accuracy and standard deviation for three training runs. Lines 1--2 (L1--L2) show unsupervised performance, i.e., individual PVPs without any training ; we give both average results across all PVPs (avg) and results for the PVP that works best on the test set (max). The large difference between both rows highlights the importance of coping with the fact that without looking at the test set, we have no means of evaluating which PVPs perform well. Zero-shot iPet clearly outperforms the unsupervised baselines for all datasets (L3 vs L1); on AG's News, it even performs better than standard supervised training with 1000 examples (L3 vs L13). With just 10 training examples, standard supervised learning does not perform above chance (L4). In contrast, Pet (L5) performs much better than the fully unsupervised baselines (L1--L2); training multiple generations using iPet (L6) gives consistent improvements. As we increase the training set size, the performance gains of Pet and iPet become smaller, but for both 50 and 100 examples, Pet continues to considerably outperform standard supervised training (L8 vs L7, L11 vs L10) with iPet (L9, L12) still giving consistent improvements. Auxiliary Language Modeling We analyze the influence of the auxiliary language modeling task on Pet's performance. Figure shows performance improvements from adding the language modeling task for four training set sizes. We see that the auxiliary task is extremely valuable when training on just 10 examples. With more data, it becomes less important, sometimes even leading to worse performance. Only for MNLI, we find language modeling to consistently help. Iterative Pet To check whether iPet is able to improve models over multiple generations, Figure shows the average performance of all generations of models in a zero-shot setting. Each additional iteration does indeed further improve the ensemble's performance. We did not investigate whether continuing this process for even more iterations gives further improvements. Another natural question is whether similar results can be obtained with fewer iterations by increasing the training set size more aggressively. To answer this question, we skip generations 2 and 3 for AG's News and Yahoo and for both tasks directly let ensemble annotate examples for . As indicated in Figure through dashed lines, this clearly leads to worse performance, highlighting the importance of only gradually increasing the training set size. We surmise that this is the case because annotating too many examples too early leads to a large percentage of mislabeled training examples. In-Domain Pretraining Unlike our supervised baseline, Pet makes use of the additional unlabeled dataset . Thus, at least some of Pet's performance gains over the supervised baseline may arise from this additional in-domain data. To test this hypothesis, we simply further pretrain RoBERTa on in-domain data, a common technique for improving text classification accuracy . As language model pretraining is expensive in terms of GPU usage, we do so only for the Yelp dataset. Figure shows results of supervised learning and Pet both with and without this in-domain pretraining. While pretraining does indeed improve accuracy for supervised training, the supervised model still clearly performs worse than Pet, showing that the success of our method is not simply due to the usage of additional unlabeled data. sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: We have shown that providing task descriptions to pretrained language models can be combined with standard supervised training. Our proposed method, Pet, consists of defining pairs of cloze question patterns and verbalizers that help leverage the knowledge contained within pretrained language models for downstream tasks. We finetune models for all pattern-verbalizer pairs and use them to create large annotated datasets on which standard classifiers can be trained. When the initial amount of training data is limited, Pet gives large improvements over standard supervised training and strong semi-supervised approaches.
